competitors.title: Server-Level vs Tool-Level Authorization | Arcade Docs
key_points: Two-tier authorization model: Resource Server Auth (front-door MCP server access) and Tool-Level Authorization (third-party API access)
Resource Server Auth authenticates every HTTP request to your MCP server via Authorization Server (WorkOS, Auth0)
Tool-Level Authorization handles user access to external services via Arcade authorization platform
Server-level auth required for HTTP servers in production; tool-level required for tools accessing user data from APIs
Configuration: MCPApp(auth=resource_server) for server-level, @app.tool(requires_auth=GitHub(...)) for tool-level

competitors.title: Contextual Access | Arcade Docs
key_points: Contextual Access powered by Logic Extensions — hooks into Arcade's execution flow at three predefined points
Access Hook: controls tool visibility per user based on role, team, entitlement, or IDP signals
Pre-Execution Hook: allows, denies, or modifies inputs before each tool execution
Post-Execution Hook: allows, denies, or modifies outputs after tool execution
Enables policy enforcement (block domains, require org-scoped inputs), payload transformation (inject secrets, redact PII), and audit routing

competitors.title: Secure Auth in Production | Arcade Docs
key_points: Two verifier options: Arcade user verifier (for prototyping/solo projects) and custom user verifier (for multi-user production)
Arcade user verifier requires users to sign in to Arcade.dev account; succeeds silently if already signed in
Custom user verifier requires building a public route accepting browser redirect with flow_id from query string
User ID must match between app session and authorization flow start; uses client.auth.confirmUser() API
Default OAuth apps only work with Arcade user verifier; production multi-user apps need own OAuth app credentials

competitors.title: User Sources | Arcade Docs
key_points: User Sources plug existing OIDC identity providers (Entra ID, Okta, Auth0, Clerk, Stytch) into MCP Gateways
Separate from Arcade admin sign-in — distinguishes end users from Arcade administrators
Project-bound: one Source can back multiple gateways, reusing the same end-user identity system
Supports Authorization Code flow with PKCE; configurable scopes and subject claims
Supports client secret rotation, deactivation (with gateway dependency checks), and deletion

competitors.title: How to manage multi-user AI agent authentication and authorization in 2026
key_points: Core design principle: treat every agent action as delegated user access, never as agent's own blanket access
Two-identity model: project-level key (agent application) + user-level identity (actual person), evaluated per action at runtime
Identity intersection rule: effective authority = strict intersection of agent permissions AND user permissions, never the union

Nine capabilities for production multi-user auth: model user/agent/context, separate OIDC from OAuth, short-lived scoped tokens, vault tokens, enforce approval steps, evaluate policy per call, just-in-time consent, bind first-time auth, immutable audit logs
OAuth 2.1 + OIDC + MCP runtime (Arcade) for delegated execution context with RFC 8707, 8693, 9449 (DPoP), 9126, 9396 compliance

competitors.title: Agent Vulnerabilities Keep Evolving, Agentic AI Security Architecture Has to Keep Up
key_points: Arcade raised $60M Series A from SYN Ventures, Morgan Stanley, and Wipro for enterprise agent security
Three attack classes documented at IEEE S&P 2026: Cross-user OAuth Session Fixation (COSF), Cross-tenant COAT, Cross-tenant Client ID Confusion
Trust inheritance problem: once OAuth relationships established, trust can be weaponized if any layer compromised
Arcade stores OAuth tokens encrypted at application layer with per-operation randomness for salting
Access control enforced at data layer, not just application layer; every token read/write requires verified match across tenant, project, and account
